title: Are You a Control Freak?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece draws a sharp distinction between healthy, results-oriented control and the dysfunctional over-control that undermines teams. The author argues that wanting to control the details that drive success is a normal, even admirable, trait shared by high achievers across disciplines. Problems arise when a leader tries to control matters that rightfully belong to someone else because of that person's greater skill or knowledge in the area. That overreach turns engaged contributors into passive order-takers who lose motivation and stop caring about outcomes. The piece closes by urging leaders not to be ashamed of wanting to control what legitimately falls under their responsibility, while explicitly letting go of what does not.
points: Wanting to control outcomes and hold people accountable is not the same as being a 'control freak' — it is a normal trait of high achievers.
Dysfunction begins when a leader tries to control things a team member is better positioned to own, given their skill or knowledge.
Over-controlling leaders turn active contributors into passive spectators who merely comply rather than engage.
The fix is not to abandon control altogether, but to ask questions and offer input rather than dictate on matters others rightly own.
Leaders should feel free to stay controlling about the details that matter, while consciously releasing control over what isn't theirs to hold.
quotes: Those who create extraordinary results often focus on controlling the details that contribute to success and desired outcomes.
The need for control is a necessary quality common to achievers and leaders in every discipline, sport, and enterprise.
Good leaders don’t control things they shouldn’t — things that others are rightly responsible for.
By exerting control over virtually all tasks and details, Control Freaks turn an active team into passive spectators who merely comply with a leader’s heavy-handed demands.
Leaders who control the details create tremendous value for themselves and the team.
Controlling everything might seem like a recipe for success, but all it really does is rob others of accountability and their need to own the outcomes, as well.
Control Freak” is a badge of disempowerment. Don’t be a freak.
